RESEARCH & IDEAS


Research directions, potential applications, and real-world use cases across the Lab’s two complementary pillars. These are ideas for investigation, not completed studies or announced projects.

title: Research
text:
Governance of AI
Understanding how AI systems should be assessed, governed, and held accountable.


Accountability, safety, and oversight


Research question
How can institutions evaluate AI systems, identify risks, and remain accountable for AI-assisted decisions?

  Social Welfare
  Public Administration



Illustrative use case
A government agency uses AI to help review applications for social assistance. What safeguards, explanations, and appeal mechanisms should protect people affected by its recommendations?




Evidence and real-world impact


Research question
How can we distinguish claims of AI effectiveness from reliable evidence about its actual consequences?

  Healthcare



Illustrative use case
A hospital introduces AI-assisted clinical decision support. Does it improve outcomes for patients, or only perform well on a test dataset? How could researchers assess the difference?

title: Research
text:
AI for Governance
Exploring the design and evaluation of AI systems that could improve institutional work, public policy, and human decision-making.


Human-AI decision-making


Research question
How should people and AI systems work together when institutional decisions have important consequences?

  Regulatory Oversight



Illustrative use case
A regulator uses an AI agent to flag cases for review. How should staff verify its recommendations, correct mistakes, and retain control over final decisions?




AI tools for policy and regulatory work


Research question
What kinds of AI tools could help institutions analyze evidence, monitor developments, or improve public-sector processes?

  Public Policy



Illustrative use case
A policy team needs to examine thousands of consultation submissions. Could an AI tool organize recurring themes and supporting evidence while keeping its findings traceable to the original documents?

title: Research
text:
Connecting Research and Implementation
A research question may lead to a policy analysis, an empirical evaluation, a prototype, or a collaboration with another institution. Some projects may involve Design → Develop → Evaluate; others may focus on one stage. Governance considerations and evidence quality matter throughout.
The Lab draws on AI, machine learning, statistics, econometrics, causal inference, economics, public policy, decision science, and software engineering. Methods should follow the questions being investigated.
Explore existing projects →

All use cases are hypothetical examples, not commissioned work or existing deployments. Research topics and possible collaborations remain open to refinement.

title: AI Impact Self-Assessment
text:
An illustrative self-assessment journey

An illustrative organizational user journey, not a replacement for any framework’s formal assessment process. AI could assist with organizing and reviewing information at each stage; users validate its suggestions and retain control of the conclusions.




01SCOPE


Describe your AI system


Describe the deployed system, its users, and its claimed societal or environmental benefits. A human confirms the scope before proceeding.


System · Users · Intended benefits



↓



02EVIDENCE


Gather supporting evidence


Upload documentation and gather stakeholder input. AI could organize sources and suggest missing information; people verify the record.


Documentation · Stakeholders · Evidence



↓



03ASSESSMENT


Assess its potential impacts


Use framework-based questions on impact, governance, human rights, and social, environmental and economic sustainability. AI could help navigate questions; humans assess the evidence.


Benefits · Harms · Trade-offs



↓



04FINDINGS


Identify risks and evidence gaps


AI could flag unsupported claims, inconsistencies and missing perspectives. Reviewers check those flags and identify unresolved harms and trade-offs.


Uncertainty · Missing evidence · Risks



↓



05OUTPUT


Receive your assessment summary


Review an AI-assisted draft of provisional findings, evidence gaps and next steps. Human approval and possible independent review remain necessary.


Impact snapshot · Priorities · External review

title: AI Impact Self-Assessment
text:
What comes out of it?

Not a certificate that an AI system is “good,” but a clearer starting point for responsible decisions.




OUTPUT 01


Provisional impact profile


A human-reviewed, provisional account of intended benefits, documented effects, possible harms, and open questions.




OUTPUT 02


Evidence & perspective gaps


Potentially AI-flagged gaps and inconsistencies, linked to sources for human verification.




OUTPUT 03


Next-step roadmap


Suggested actions for evidence collection, safeguards, stakeholder engagement, and independent evaluation, confirmed by people.





↗


Why independent perspectives still matter
An organization assessing its own system may overlook harms or overstate benefits. AI-generated suggestions can also be incomplete or misleading. This proposed tool is a preparatory and reflective aid, not a certification or substitute for independent assessment. Human reviewers must check evidence, consider affected stakeholders, and make normative judgments. Rigorous frameworks such as HIIG’s Impact AI Method additionally rely on interviews, qualitative analysis, and external involvement.

title: AI Impact Self-Assessment
section: Towards an Integrated AI Impact Assessment Framework
text:
Towards an Integrated AI Impact Assessment Framework

The five-step self-assessment above illustrates one component of a broader research agenda. I am interested in developing an AI-assisted platform across three complementary pillars, with human oversight and independent perspectives throughout.




POTENTIAL RESEARCH PLATFORM


AI-assisted impact assessment


Framework-informed · Evidence-oriented · Human-in-the-loop




01 · STRUCTURED ASSESSMENT Evidence & stakeholder perspectives Framework-guided review of documentation, interviews, governance, and potential harms (e.g., HIIG’s Impact AI Method). What do we know and how credible is the evidence?


02 · QUANTITATIVE Data & causal evaluation Operational and observational data, descriptive statistics, experiments, and causal designs when appropriate. Did deploying the AI system cause a change in outcomes?


03 · INSTITUTIONAL Use & accountability Human review, institutional adoption, governance, and decisions informed by findings. Does the assessment improve decisions and accountability?

title: About
text:
ABOUT



AI Governance Lab is an independent, early-stage research and technology initiative working at the intersection of artificial intelligence, human decision-making, governance, and public policy.
Its mission is to advance governance and public policy through the design, development, and rigorous evaluation of AI systems. The Lab aims to connect empirical research with practical technology, without separating the building of AI systems from examining their benefits, risks, and real-world effects.

title: From AI Claims to Evidence
section: Research case study: Can AI make hiring fairer?
text:
Research case study: Can AI make hiring fairer?

One possible research direction. AI-assisted recruitment is a useful test case because AI developers (such as companies providing automated CV screening and candidate-ranking tools) may claim that their systems make hiring fairer, while applicants, employers, and regulators need to know whether the evidence supports those claims.




ILLUSTRATIVE CLAIM


“Our AI system reduces discrimination in hiring.”


What would we need to know before relying on this claim?




01 · EVIDENCE What was actually measured? Suppose a vendor reports 90% prediction accuracy and a completed bias audit. We would ask: accuracy on which applicants, against which labels, with what subgroup results, and under what testing conditions? A performance score alone does not establish fairer hiring.


02 · INFERENCE Does the evidence support the claim? Were error rates and selection outcomes compared across relevant groups? Is the sample representative of actual applicants? To claim the system reduces discrimination, what credible comparison with hiring without the system is available? Association, prediction, and causal impact are different.


03 · GOVERNANCE What should decision-makers do? Should an employer request more documentation, commission an independent audit, pilot the tool with safeguards, monitor outcomes, or avoid deployment until the evidence improves? The evidentiary standard should match the decision and stakes.




Why this matters in practice: Governments are already confronting these questions.

In the UK, official guidance discusses evidence of bias audits, while the Information Commissioner’s Office has investigated AI recruitment tools.
In the US, New York City’s Local Law 144 requires bias audits and public summaries of their results for covered automated employment decision tools.
Meanwhile, the EU AI Act classifies certain AI systems used in recruitment as high-risk, establishing additional requirements for their providers and deployers.

These examples raise a common research question: What evidence is sufficient to demonstrate that an AI system is fair, reliable, and suitable for real-world use?
Potential research output:

A comparative study of publicly documented claims about fairness in AI-assisted recruitment, examining the evidence used to support them, the strength of the conclusions that can be drawn, and the implications for governance.
The study could produce a structured evidence matrix and a policy paper identifying gaps in current evaluation practices and recommending ways to improve transparency, accountability, and regulatory oversight.

title: From AI Claims to Evidence
section: How the Research Project Approaches the Problem
text:
How the Research Project Approaches the Problem

This project is built around three interconnected questions: how to assess the credibility of evidence about AI systems, determine what conclusions it supports, and translate those findings into informed governance decisions.




01EVIDENCE QUALITY


What makes AI governance evidence credible?


How should decision-makers assess the provenance, independence, limitations, and reproducibility of developer claims, evaluations, audits, and incident reports? Which claims are actually supported?


Sources · Incentives · Validation · Uncertainty



↓



02MEASUREMENT


What do evaluations tell us about real-world outcomes?


Under what assumptions do benchmark results, pre-deployment tests, monitoring data, and observed incidents generalize to real-world risks or benefits? Where could statistical or causal methods improve inference?


External validity · Measurement · Causal identification



↓



03GOVERNANCE


When should evidence change a governance decision?


What evidence thresholds and escalation procedures could inform deployment, monitoring, disclosure, independent evaluation, or regulatory intervention? How should institutions act when uncertainty remains substantial?


Decision thresholds · Accountability · Trade-offs

title: From AI Claims to Evidence
text:
How We Investigate These Questions

This project combines policy research, comparative case studies, and quantitative analysis to examine how AI-related claims are supported by evidence and how that evidence can inform governance decisions.




METHOD 01


Map evidence requirements


Compare public evaluation, assurance, and governance approaches; identify which decisions they support and what information they require.




METHOD 02


Analyze selected cases


Trace claims to underlying evidence in a small, transparent sample; code gaps, uncertainty, incentives, and limitations. Interviews are optional and subject to access.




METHOD 03


Test decision implications


Develop a decision-focused comparison of evidence thresholds or review triggers; use quantitative analysis only where justified by the available evidence.





↗


Research integrity and limits
A model-generated summary is not independent verification. An audit is not necessarily evidence of real-world safety, and an observed association is not necessarily a causal effect. This concept calls for traceable sources, explicit assumptions, consideration of affected parties, and clear separation between empirical findings and normative judgments. No evidence collection, interviews, model evaluations, or empirical validation have been completed for this concept.

title: From AI Claims to Evidence
text:
From Research to Policy Recommendations


EXPECTED CONTRIBUTION


Central question: What evidence should decision-makers require before relying on claims about AI systems?
This project aims to translate research into actionable insights for AI governance. An initial contribution could be a comparative study of publicly documented AI evaluation and assurance practices, examining the credibility of supporting evidence, identifying gaps and limitations, and assessing their implications for governance decisions.
The research could produce a policy paper or research report, accompanied by a structured evidence matrix that documents the supporting evidence, its limitations, and the conclusions it can reasonably support. Together, these outputs would offer practical recommendations for strengthening transparency, accountability, and regulatory oversight.
